name: Starting Solids: BLW & Purees — Palina Baltsevich
buyer: Parent starting solids who wants preparation guidance, a food diary and caregiver sharing.
mechanism: Age-specific food cards with a shareable food diary
price: US App Store lists $7.99/$9.99 monthly, $29.99/$59.99 annual and other SKUs; applicable offer unknown
format: App food cards, photos, guides, food/reaction diary; supports BLW, purées or mixed feeding.
inputs: Age bands, foods tried, favorites and reactions; no household shopping/budget planner demonstrated in description.
promise: Reduce preparation uncertainty and make food history available to partners, caregivers and pediatricians.
proof: Developer description and displayed ratings, not an independent clinical or purchasing assessment.
objections: Different feeding approaches, practical serving questions and subscription cancellation.
comparison: Caregiver sharing is already available. It can be part of a report's usefulness but cannot be claimed as an unoccupied differentiator.
gaps: No app or subscription tested. Store age rating is a content rating, not the baby's age or evidence of minor customers.
quote: A FOOD DIARY YOU CAN SHARE

name: Annabel Karmel — recipes, first foods and custom planners
buyer: Parent moving from first tastes to shared family meals and wanting simple planning.
mechanism: Recipe collections and feedback feed custom meal planners
price: US App Store lists AK Monthly $5.99 and AK Annual $39.99; seven-day trial stated
format: App with 1,500-plus recipes, first-food preparation, tracking, advice and planners.
inputs: Age/stage, search filters, favorites/collections, recipe feedback and foods/reactions logged. Automatic questionnaire-generated month plan not demonstrated.
promise: Make family feeding and recipe selection easier with ongoing ideas.
proof: Brand claims decades of expertise and broad family use; no independent efficacy or subscriber validation.
objections: Finding appropriate recipes, what to cook, food variety and practical record keeping.
comparison: Ordinary custom planning and baby-to-family recipes have established alternatives. A report must prove lower effort than selecting recipes here.
gaps: Original website excluded under GPTBot robots rule; inspected developer's permitted US App Store page instead. No paid flow tested.

name: My Little Food Critic — weekly planner and shopping app
buyer: Parent wanting recipes that work for baby and family, including dietary substitutions.
mechanism: Recipe selection builds weekly menus and shopping lists
price: US App Store MLFC Monthly $3.99; website still says £1.49/$1.49 monthly; unresolved discrepancy
format: Recipes, weekly planner, automatic shopping list, first-food guide, instructional videos and play content.
inputs: Diet/allergy filters, ingredients or recipe names, favorites, chosen weekly recipes and family shopping extras.
promise: Make varied family cooking more accessible while reducing separate recipe searching.
proof: Seller descriptions and founder account; displayed review sample is not representative of all customers.
objections: Food restrictions, cooking time, units and finding usable recipes.
comparison: Household dietary filters, quick-meal categories and grocery consolidation already exist. Their presence challenges a generic household-tailored PDF proposition.
gaps: Applicable price/checkout not tested; the website's publication copy appears older than its App Store offer. No generated plan inspected.
quote: automatically create a shopping list from the recipes

name: My Little Food Critic — 28-Day Meal Plan
buyer: Parent at the start of solids wanting a bounded step-by-step plan.
mechanism: Four-week guide combines purées and finger-food serving
price: Live localized product page €34.95; indexed UK result £27.99 not independently confirmed in checkout
format: Guide with a 100-plus-first-foods tracker bonus; digital delivery inferred from requires_shipping:false in saved HTML, exact file unobserved.
inputs: Product page shows only default product variant. No individualized household intake observed.
promise: Help parents start with variety/flavor and know how to serve foods using their chosen feeding approach.
proof: Seller product description; no clinical outcome or verified purchase dataset inspected.
objections: Purées versus finger foods: supports either or both; says there are no hard-and-fast food-order rules.
comparison: Direct substitute for a first-30-days report, even without customization. A fixed duration alone is therefore not a distinctive offer structure.
gaps: Paid contents, exact file/fulfillment and applicable currency not tested. No evidence of how many buyers pay this price.

name: BabyPlate — culturally filtered weekly solids guidance
buyer: First-time parent starting solids, including families using halal, kosher or plant-based diets.
mechanism: Diet setup and food logs adapt weekly suggestions
price: US App Store lists Premium Monthly $14.99, yearly $79.99 and other offers/terms; checkout untested
format: Food database/cards, food/reaction history, weekly guidance and caregiver sharing.
inputs: Baby age, feeding approach, diet preferences/allergies and foods/reactions logged. Listing explicitly names halal, kosher, vegan and vegetarian filters.
promise: Make weekly choices and preparation less confusing while coordinating food history.
proof: Developer claims specialist input and guideline alignment; these are not independently appraised. Its specific allergen-protocol assertions are not clinical evidence.
objections: Different feeding methods, cultural diet fit, tracking and caregiver consistency.
comparison: Culturally relevant personalization and adaptation to prior foods are already claimed. Do not position either as a discovery of empty market space.
gaps: No app, religious-diet compliance, plan quality or medical claims verified. Subscription covers access; free download is not free feature access.

name: Little Lunches — household meal plans and grocery integration
buyer: Family with a baby starting solids and other household members to feed.
mechanism: Family preferences generate menus and consolidated grocery lists
price: Official web page $7.99/month or $49.99/year; free plan preview; platform/location differences flagged
format: Weekly age-based plans, recipes, grocery lists/pantry tools, cooking tutorials, caregiver access and delivery links.
inputs: Family age groups from six months, meal slots, allergies/restrictions and changing preferences; ingredient reuse described.
promise: Reduce planning/shopping work and make one family's food requirements manageable.
proof: Seller describes pediatric/dietitian/chef involvement and large family counts; actual outcomes/usage not audited.
objections: Different diets/ages, planning only selected meals, later changes, portions and groceries.
comparison: The clearest counterexample to an assumed gap in household-specific first-solids planning. It already claims much of the proposed input/output bundle.
gaps: No generated menu, onboarding completion, grocery checkout or clinical quality tested. A portable report could still suit some buyers; preference is unproven.

name: BLW Recipes by Orango Labs — generated 1–100-day plans
buyer: Parent wanting a plan of selectable duration that fits family diet and avoids recorded allergens.
mechanism: Generate chosen-duration menus with diet filters and groceries
price: US App Store lists monthly $9.99, annual $29.99 and lifetime $9.99/$19.99 SKUs; applicable offer unknown
format: App food/recipe library, tracking, 1–100-day plan generator and grocery list; three-day Pro trial stated.
inputs: Age, meal, skill level, family diet, allergens and chosen date range; manual meal-by-meal editing advertised.
promise: Make choosing, tracking and shopping for first foods easier.
proof: Developer description. Store has insufficient ratings for an overview; no evidence of commercial traction or validated plan quality.
objections: Diet fit, plan duration, privacy and account burden; description says no account needed and data stays on device.
comparison: Direct feature collision with a personalized first-30-days report. Low-price/lifetime SKUs are competitive signals, not proof of an available checkout or sales.
gaps: No generated plan, specialist credentials, safety or actual local data handling inspected. A newly visible app can show imitation risk without proving demand.
quote: Generate 1 day to 100 days in one tap
